1000-words.deck: On the way to Olympus, the gods hand you a tablet full of jumbled letters and start the clock.

overview.text: Move the cursor across the tablet to build words out of jumbled letters. In one challenge, you have six tries to unscramble a particular word. The gods can hit you with a lightning bolt that hides letters or cuts the time you have left.
Quickplay lets you pick timed word-building, a limited-guess six-letter puzzle, or a round that calls for words of particular lengths.

development.text: Mathieu Boisvert and Alexandre P. Normand led programming on the Java edition. Alexis Green-Painchaud is credited for both writing and revision, and Mathieu Vachon composed the music.

release.text: MobyGames places Gameloft’s release on 19 October 2004, the same date it lists for Babaroga’s BREW port. Gameloft still listed the game in its 2006 catalog.
Chris James compared the Java game to the television quiz Countdown in his 2006 Pocket Gamer review. The one control he found awkward was cycling through letters while a timer was running.

quotes.text: The control system can feel a little unwieldy at first, as you fritter away valuable seconds cycling through the letters.
quotes.speaker: Chris James

age-of-empires-iii.deck: Build a settlement, raise an army and give orders while the battle is paused.

overview.text: A mission starts with a few settlers and limited supplies. Gather wood, food and gold, put up a town centre and barracks, and leave enough housing for the people you train. A village with surplus supplies can trade at a market. An outpost can fire on enemy troops while your settlers keep working.
As you advance through the ages, your Home City can send you better supplies. Early shipments bring resources such as food. Later ones can send musketeers and cannons.

development.text: Glu took on Microsoft’s licence after In-Fusio had adapted Age of Empires II for phones. The third game gives a single cursor several jobs. Tap a map square to move a unit, open a unit’s menu to give it a job, or double-select a soldier to command the division. You can pause, issue orders and watch the troops carry them out when play resumes.

release.text: Pocket Gamer reported the licence in March 2007 and initially expected the game in 2008. Kath Brice reviewed the Java game in September 2007. Glu’s later North American lineup put Age of Empires III in February 2009 and confirmed plans for an N-Gage edition.

studio_roles.name: Glu Mobile
studio_roles.role: Licensed mobile adaptation, development and publishing

ancient-empires.deck: Fight for castles and mountain passes in Macrospace’s turn-based campaign for Java phones.

overview.text: King Galamar leads his troops against his twin brother Valadorn. A mountain gives a unit more protection than open ground, and towns or castles heal troops and generate gold. When two groups fight, the map gives way to a close-up of both squads.
You can save partway through a mission and return to the same battle, even with soldiers spread across the map.

release.text: The Guardian was already reviewing the game in January 2004. MobyGames lists a January 12 Java release, while GameSpot’s U.S. listing gives March 4.

ancient-empires-ii.deck: Galamar and Valadorn fight side by side against an enemy that knows how to gang up on a weakened unit.

overview.text: The brothers from the first game team up to keep Saeth from taking control of Thorin. Across eight missions, a catapult can knock down a building and infantry can repair it and claim the site. Enemy units can work together, so leaving a wounded soldier exposed can cost a turn’s worth of progress.
Alongside the campaign, the Java game has a skirmish mode where up to four people can take turns in the same fight.

release.text: The UK Java release is listed in June 2005, with Macrospace as developer and Glu Mobile as publisher. In February 2006, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences named it Cellular Game of the Year.

quotes.text: we discovered after reaching mission four, where we soundly got beaten nine times in a row.
quotes.speaker: Keith Stuart
quotes.attribution: GameSpot, on the sequel’s challenge in its June 2005 mobile review

aporkalypse-pigs-of-doom.deck: HandyGames’ isometric puzzles send four pigs to close the gates of heaven and hell.

overview.text: The four pigs work as a team. Hunger can swallow an object and drop it somewhere useful. War fires at targets, Pest can possess enemies, and Death can teleport to a fallen enemy. A route through a level can take several of those abilities in turn.

release.text: HandyGames made and published the Java edition. MobyGames records it on Nokia’s Ovi Store and on Jamba or Jamster in December 2010. In April 2011, Pocket Gamer reported that HandyGames planned to bring the game to Xperia Play.

asphalt-3-3d-street-rules.deck: Race recklessly enough and the camera can pull up into the news helicopter following you.

overview.text: You can race for first place, wreck opponents in Beat-Em All, or string together stunts in Cash Attack. Upgrades adjust how your car drives and your passenger brings a bonus, such as less police attention or better coverage from the news crew.

development.text: The team used the 3D version’s moving camera to change the viewpoint during a chase. When a news helicopter turns up, the camera briefly follows the race from above. Gameloft says that new angle meant the cars and scenery needed enough detail to hold up from more than one viewpoint.

release.text: Pocket Gamer reported on 22 March 2007 that the 3D edition could be bought directly from Gameloft. The Java release date is separate from the original 2D Street Rules in 2006 and from subsequent BREW and N-Gage service editions.

asphalt-urban-gt.deck: Gameloft’s 2D Java racer let the car handle the throttle while you steered, braked and looked for nitro.

overview.text: New York and Paris share the route list with Luxor, Syracuse and Vladivostok. In the Java game you can knock rivals around and spend your winnings on new cars, but the more damage you cause, the more likely you are to face roadblocks or a police helicopter.

development.text: Gameloft remembers considering open-wheel racing, rally and stock cars before choosing illegal street racing. The game’s Java credits name Philippe Laurens as producer and Sylvain Rouquette as lead programmer. Auto-acceleration left the player free to steer, brake and hit nitro on a phone keypad.

release.text: The 2D Java version arrived in December 2004. GameSpot reviewed it that month, and Pocket Gamer followed in February. Gameloft briefly reissued the Java game in a browser for the series’ 2020 anniversary.

quotes.text: You really do zoom along, with scenery whipping past at a rapid pace
quotes.speaker: Stuart Dredge

assassin-s-creed.deck: Gameloft put Altaïr in a side-scrolling adventure where timing a single keypress could get him across a rooftop gap.

overview.text: Altaïr adds a grappling hook and crossbow to his sword as he works his way through Gameloft’s Third Crusade platformer. The crossbow can disarm mechanisms as well as hit enemies.

development.text: The Java game simplifies some awkward keypad moves into one timed press. Pocket Gamer’s Chris Maddox describes a tutorial that stops play at a chasm and prompts you to press 2 or up. Altaïr makes the diagonal leap and catches the far ledge.
The Nokia N70 credit transcription names Zhang Bo Liang as lead game designer and Arthur Hugot and Lu Hai Jia as graphics managers. This credit group belongs to the phone game.

release.text: Gameloft released teaser shots in October 2007, followed by an announcement promising 13 missions across four settings. Pocket Gamer reviewed the Java game on 5 November. Maddox enjoyed the platforming and thought there was less stealth than he had expected.

quotes.text: It's great fun sprinting and jumping across a chasm of spikes
quotes.speaker: Chris Maddox

avalanche-snowboarding.deck: Tuck for speed, charge your jump before the lip and use the directional keys for tricks in the air.

overview.text: Avalanche Snowboarding turns the descent into an arcade run through rails, cabins and cliffs. Hold the jump key on the approach, release it at the ramp and hit a direction to throw a trick. An especially large jump can be the way over a chasm.

release.text: Gameloft Argentina and Gameloft Software Shanghai made the Java release. MobyGames dates it to January 2010, and Pocket Gamer reviewed it on January 29.

bioshock.deck: IG Fun redraws Rapture from above, with the original story told through a keypad action game.

overview.text: The 2D phone adaptation tells the story of the first BioShock. IG Fun kept recognisable spaces, plasmids and the encounter with the Big Daddy, but moved the action to an overhead view. Audio diaries and radio messages carry pieces of the story between fights.

development.text: Executive producer Hrishi Oberoi said the artists kept the curves of Rapture’s architecture and used standing water, leaks and glimpses outside to keep the city’s setting in view. They tried softer and harder shadows and used sound effects at particular points. IG Fun also worked with 2K to cut down the story, planning three separate instalments.
CEO Sean Malatesta was already showing footage on a BREW handset in 2008. That demo was the separate 3D conversion. He described the 2D game as a version for phones that could not run the 3D project.

release.text: Pocket Gamer published its Java review on March 20, 2009. At GDC a few days later, Malatesta was still discussing distribution of the 2D and 3D conversions to providers. The review gives a date for the press build, while carrier-level rollout dates and shipments of later chapters need separate evidence.

quotes.text: One of our biggest challenges was the visualisation of the BioShock world in a two dimensional perspective.
quotes.speaker: Hrishi Oberoi
quotes.attribution: Pocket Gamer interview with Jon Mundy, March 24, 2009

studio_roles.name: 2K
studio_roles.role: Worked with IG Fun on adapting the story

bounce-tales.deck: Rovio’s bouncing-ball platformer came preloaded on Nokia phones such as the X3 and X2.

overview.text: The colours of Sky Bean Land are disappearing into a series of machines. Bounce tracks them down by rolling and jumping through obstacles. Later he can turn into a heavy ball that breaks through walls or a light ball that jumps higher.

development.text: Rovio made the game for Nokia when it was taking on contract work for other companies. A community study of the code identifies graphics and device-control interfaces specific to Nokia’s Java implementation.

release.text: MobyGames dates the Rovio-developed, Nokia-published Java release to 2008. Nokia’s 2009 X3 and 2010 X2 product sheets document later preloads.

castlevania-order-of-shadows.deck: A new Belmont story for carrier phones with a score that had to fit the limits of each stage.

overview.text: Order of Shadows was an original mobile Castlevania, developed alongside Konami’s separate plans for a phone edition of Aria of Sorrow. Tyrone Rodriguez led the design. The game had its own storyline, music and approach to abilities, with collaboration from series producer Koji Igarashi.

development.text: Vincent Diamante wrote the score in SP-MIDI, which let sounds drop out when a handset could only play a few notes at once. The same patch also sounded different across phone makers, and each stage had a small MIDI file budget. He had to trim notes, bends and volume changes, sometimes until the result became a substantially different piece.
Konami’s Developers Corner opened with a post from Rodriguez. Chris Kohler linked to the blog at launch and described it as containing sketches and notes from the team.

release.text: Konami announced September 18 for major US carriers and clarified the initial announcement's geography. On September 25, WIRED reported that Konami was announcing availability. Kohler’s earlier review was played on a Verizon V-Cast phone. He liked the controls and music but thought the game fell short of what series fans would want.

quotes.text: I could only really afford to have super active files really dense with note data on very short loops.
quotes.speaker: Vincent Diamante
quotes.attribution: Interview with Video Game Music Online

credits.name: Koji Igarashi
credits.scope: Original mobile project, duty beyond collaboration unspecified by the launch announcement

company-of-heroes.deck: The Java adaptation puts Able Company’s Normandy campaign on a turn-based grid.

overview.text: Pick the units for a mission and deploy them before the first turn. A cursor and colour-coded grid show where each unit can move or fire. Buildings and shell craters provide cover, and some objectives call for holding ground through a counterattack.

development.text: Viva La Mobile developed the Java release for THQ Wireless. The mobile credits put John Murphy in both production and development, with David Kainer in production, Tony Schofield and Ian Hosken in development, and James Croke and Jeremy Kupsch in art.

Artist Bill Harbison supplied Java mock-ups to Games That Weren’t in 2024. His name appears in the Java credits for Worms 2007. The surviving evidence leaves open how his Company of Heroes artwork relates to the Viva La Mobile release.

release.text: Pocket Gamer announced a turn-based phone game in August 2006 and reviewed the Java release that November. Games That Weren’t later discussed the mock-ups as potentially unreleased work. The contemporary review and Java credits document a released adaptation.

quotes.text: It's all very simple, with colour-coded grids showing ranges and potential targets.
quotes.speaker: Mike Abolins

contra-4.deck: The DS game's phone adaptation swaps in a fan-designed soldier and redraws the action for one screen.

overview.text: Bill Rizer returns, and Solomon Caesar takes the other playable slot. Konami invited mobile players to design a character in 2007 and put the winning design into the release. The Java version is single-player and breaks the DS stages into shorter sections. The two-screen and pseudo-3D sections were left out.

development.text: Contra Encyclopedia documents several Java variants. They differ in graphics, sound and the arrangement of levels depending on the handset. On the tested Java builds, the character fires automatically. Composer Vincent Diamante recalls doing phone soundtracks at Konami, with Contra 4 among the titles he names.

release.text: Pocket Gamer reported the game was already out in the US on November 20, 2007. Its October 2008 report describes the game's introduction to Sprint through a new Konami carrier deal. That later deal is separate from the initial US mobile rollout.

crash-bandicoot-mutant-island.deck: Crash swings on vines, slides down slopes and takes control of Titans big enough to fill several screens.

overview.text: Cortex has hypnotised the bandicoots, so Crash opens up routes, finds switches and rescues them as he moves across the island. Some stages end with an enormous Titan. Beat it and Crash can ride it through the next stretch.

release.text: Glu announced Mutant Island in June 2009 as part of its expanded licensing deal with Activision. Pocket Gamer reviewed the Java game in July and names Vivendi Games Mobile as developer. GameFAQs records Glu’s US release on 30 July.

notes.text: MobyGames records a separate 2008 listing with Vivendi as publisher. Its carrier and availability remain unverified.

quotes.text: The end-of-level bosses, meanwhile, are impressively rendered Titans that stand several screens tall.
quotes.speaker: Jon Mundy

critter-crunch.deck: Feed a small critter to a bigger one, then use the bigger one to set off a chain reaction.

overview.text: Biggs snatches critters with his tongue and feeds them back into the rows creeping down the screen. Overfill one and its neighbours of the same colour can burst too. Adventure mode keeps the rows coming, while Puzzle mode gives you a fixed number of moves to clear the board.

development.text: Capybara spent about a month making a prototype before getting the go-ahead. The programmers could switch individual rules on and off to test different combinations, and the designers used an in-house editor to build levels. The team also made a tool to help port its J2ME games to BREW.

Vic Nguyen drew and animated the critters, and David Hoang worked on the jungle backgrounds. Kenneth Yeung built a library of procedural effects. The Java credits also list Living Mobile Czech, whose team worked on the port.

Lead programmer Radek Koncewicz recalls one rule players struggled to follow. Neighbouring critters originally joined a chain only if they had eaten the same amount. He suggested matching by colour alone, which let players see the next link before they fed the first critter. He also added sliders to the editor so designers could tune how often blockers and powerups appeared in different levels.

release.text: Pocket Gamer reviewed Disney’s Java release in August 2007. Java release records list Starwave Mobile in the US and Living Mobile in the UK. Capybara’s mobile game won Best Game and Achievement in Art at the 2008 IGF Mobile awards.

quotes.text: Being able to try a lot of different gameplay configurations really helped us zero in on the best combination
quotes.speaker: Capybara Games
quotes.attribution: Matt Repetski, Sean Lohrisch and Kris Piotrowski in a joint interview

credits.role: Producer, level design, music and sound

studio_roles.role: Publisher credited for the UK release

deep-submarine-odyssey.deck: Your first submarine can only survive inside a narrow band of ocean. Better equipment opens the depths.

overview.text: On a flooded planet, you start out harpooning local sea life from a one-person sub. There is better money in escorting freight and clearing mines. Take jobs at submerged stations and spend the pay on weapons, thrusters and shields.
Pressure keeps a low-end submarine from diving too far, and radiation keeps it away from the surface. Buying a better craft changes which parts of the ocean and which jobs you can reach.

development.text: Fishlabs used its ABYSS engine again after Galaxy on Fire. Martin Brüning and Hans-Christian Kühl are credited with the idea, and Kühl programmed the game. The space fighter and its ports gave way to a submarine, diving limits and underwater stations.

release.text: Mobile Game FAQs lists February 22, 2007 as the release date. Pocket Gamer played a beta that February, then reviewed the game on a Sony Ericsson W810i in March. Sony Ericsson later added Deep to its Fun & Downloads deal with Fishlabs.

diamond-rush.deck: The gems are easy to spot. Getting to them without trapping yourself takes more thought.

overview.text: A single boulder can block your exit or clear a path through a trap. Red gems can be hidden, and you need enough of them to move on. The trail takes the explorer through Angkor Wat, Bavaria and Tibet, where he can use tools such as a grappling hook to pull obstacles toward him.

development.text: The Java edition credits Roc Alabern for game design. Gameloft’s Bulgarian and Spanish teams share development credit. Arthur Hugot and Florian Masereel are listed as art directors, with Toni Rodríguez and Doychin Doychev leading the graphic artists.

release.text: Michael French reviewed the Java edition in August 2006. He found that resetting a room cost a life and that the puzzles became more varied as you acquired new tools. Gameloft’s annual reference document also records favorable reviews from Cell Freak and AirGamer.

quotes.text: There's no leeway for mistakes and you're often forced to reset the area (costing you a life) to have another go.
quotes.speaker: Michael French

digital-devil-story-megami-tensei.deck: Atlus brought the Famicom dungeon crawler to Japanese Java phones in 2004.

overview.text: Akemi Nakajima and Yumiko Shirasagi descend into a maze to face Lucifer. They can fight the demons they meet or talk some into joining them. The game began as a 1987 Famicom RPG based on Aya Nishitani’s novel.

Wakka records an English J2ME copy under the same title. My Abandonware now lists English and Chinese Java copies. The English translation’s maker and date remain open, and the exact copy Wakka used has yet to be identified.

development.text: Famitsu’s launch report describes a Vodafone edition with an automap and the option to save anywhere. Atlus also adapted the game for NTT DoCoMo’s FOMA 900i. ITmedia reported that the Japanese DoJa team redrew the graphics and lowered the Famicom game’s difficulty.

release.text: Famitsu reported a December 1, 2004 launch on Vodafone Live! for five Japanese handsets, including the J-SH53. The download cost ¥525. Vodafone used its Java-based V-appli platform on that range of phones.

Earlier that year Atlus offered its FOMA version through the MegaTen α portal alongside other games and Aya Nishitani’s revised digital novels. The FOMA free trial added in April capped progression at level ten and disabled saves. A further edition appeared on BBMF’s EZweb BREW service in 2005.

credits.name: Aya Nishitani
credits.scope: Original novel and revised mobile-service digital edition

studio_roles.name: Atlus
studio_roles.role: Publisher named in the Vodafone launch report

doom-ii-rpg.deck: id Mobile returned to turn-based Doom with three selectable characters and another hostile research station.

overview.text: A distress call sends a small squad to a lunar station. You explore the corridors in real time. When you encounter a demon, deciding whether to move, shoot or use a med kit gives the enemy its own turn. Spanner Spencer described the station falling apart almost as soon as the squad arrived. He found the writing had room for jokes in between the firefights.

development.text: Jacob Enget worked on a six-person team that developed the game across several mobile platforms in ten months. He says he cut image memory in half in the low-end engine, bringing the total down by a third to fit a 300 KB budget. His résumé identifies that as work on the low-end version and does not assign the figure to every Java handset.
The sequel was among the early projects of id Mobile, the new division led by Fountainhead founder Katherine Anna Kang.

release.text: id disclosed the project at QuakeCon in August 2008. Pocket Gamer reviewed a Java build on December 17, 2009. GameFAQs gives more than one 2009 date under its general mobile grouping, so the review is a firmer Java-specific marker than those day-level dates.

credits.name: Jacob Enget
credits.scope: Multiplatform production and low-end engine optimisation

doom-rpg.deck: The Mars base advances one turn at a time in a first-person RPG built around a phone keypad.

overview.text: You still enter a Mars research base full of demons. The change is what happens after you move. Walking a tile or firing spends a turn, giving the creatures around you a chance to move or strike. Credits buy upgrades, and better health or accuracy carries forward from one sector to the next.

development.text: John Carmack started the project after trying the Java game demos on a replacement phone. Its directional pad worked for one hand, but he found it awkward for the combination of movement and fire that a Doom shooter needed. Tile-by-tile movement let him keep the first-person view without asking a player to press two controls at once.

Carmack did three stretches of programming and held design reviews. Fountainhead Entertainment carried the game through to release. In December 2005 he described a more than twentyfold performance difference between the modest Java devices they supported and the high-end BREW hardware. Java and BREW builds could share the game's design while making different demands on the handset.

release.text: In July 2005, Pocket Gamer reported that id and JAMDAT planned the game for the autumn, around the Doom film. Its Java review appeared on November 9.

quotes.text: sort of Bard’s Tale meets Doom
quotes.speaker: John Carmack
quotes.attribution: Development notes quoted by Tor Thorsen in GameSpot, March 29, 2005

driv3r.deck: Sorrent’s phone adaptation offered two steering schemes for the same stunt-filled chase.

overview.text: Undercover driver Tanner follows a car-theft ring from Miami to Nice and Istanbul. The mobile game lets you choose whether the direction pad points the car across the screen or works like an accelerator, brake and steering wheel. The second layout also gives you sharper turns using the handbrake.

development.text: Sorrent’s Jill Braff told GameSpot that the company would develop its edition in-house and promote it with Atari. Trade coverage names Robert Nashak as the newly appointed head of Sorrent’s mobile production in May 2004, with DRIV3R among the projects under his remit.

release.text: Braff described a plan to launch the phone game alongside the bigger versions, with promotion through carriers and Atari’s campaign. MobyGames dates the J2ME edition to 21 June 2004. Reviewing the phone game the next day, Stephen Palley preferred the extra control of relative steering but found the sharp corners and traffic unforgiving.

credits.name: Robert Nashak
credits.scope: Studio production oversight, contemporary trade report

edge.deck: Roll a cube through isometric mazes and use each face to climb over obstacles.

overview.text: Each direction rolls the cube onto another face. The cube can climb a step its own height. The small cubes scattered through each maze take more planning to reach than the exit does.

development.text: David Papazian dates Matthieu Malot’s rolling-cube idea to 2004 and the start of development to 2006. The two had worked at Gameloft before making the game at Mobigame. Papazian coded and produced the Java release, and Malot handled game design and graphics.

Malot and Papazian bought Rubik’s cubes and used them to try out situations away from the screen. They hoped to get Edge preloaded on phones, but a Sony Ericsson deal fell through in 2008. The iPhone release followed that December.

release.text: Mobigame first released Edge for iPhone in December 2008. It partnered with Connect2Media for the Java edition, reviewed in December 2009. The companies also announced motion controls for compatible handsets.

quotes.text: When you work on a game with cubes, you need cubes
quotes.speaker: David Papazian
quotes.attribution: Mobigame co-founder, quoted in Ryan Rigney’s Buttonless (2011)

fantasy-worlds-rhynn.deck: A free Java MMO with character classes, quests and a chat window for meeting other players.

overview.text: Choose one of four character types, then gain levels through quests and combat. Rhynn was free to play, with any data charges falling to the player. In 2010 the site BoostApps tested it on a Motorola i776 and found that reconnecting could require restarting the game.

development.text: Norbert Nopper is credited with the original concept. Jochai Papke led the project and programming, while Jan-Eric Lauble worked across game design, graphics and levels. Papke’s repository includes the client, server and worldbuilder. The README identifies the code as based on versions 1.4 and later.

release.text: MobyGames dates the Java release to October 2008 and identifies AwareDreams as the developer and macrolutions Ltd. as publisher. A server update in 2010 made client version 1.3.7 mandatory. By March 2012, BoostApps had reported that the original servers were down.
Papke identifies Rhynn-X as the revival he is involved in. OpenRhynn also uses the game’s released source and describes itself as a fan remake.

quotes.text: I’m Jochai (“marlowe”), creator and original lead developer of Fantasy Worlds: Rhynn and founder of macrolutions Ltd., the company that published it.
quotes.speaker: Jochai Papke

credits.name: Jochai Papke
credits.role: Project lead, game design and lead programming

credits.name: Jan-Eric Lauble
credits.role: Game design, graphics and level design

final-fantasy.deck: The first Final Fantasy reached US feature phones through a 2010 deal between Square Enix and Namco Networks.

overview.text: The Warriors of Light set out to restore four elemental crystals. The phone release follows the original adventure across land, sea and air, with turn-based battles along the way.

release.text: Pocket Gamer reported US availability on 15 March 2010, with Canada due to follow. Square Enix’s Takuya Okada said the licensing deal with Namco Networks covered plans beyond the first Final Fantasy.
The catalog entry follows the North American Java edition. Its source also lists distinct MSX and BREW editions under the same title.

quotes.text: Our partnership extends beyond Final Fantasy and we look forward to releasing additional games in the future.
quotes.speaker: Takuya Okada
quotes.attribution: Square Enix, quoted in Pocket Gamer, 15 March 2010

final-fantasy-iv-the-after-years.deck: Final Fantasy IV’s phone sequel gave Rydia, Edge and other returning characters episodes of their own.

overview.text: Cecil and Rosa’s son Ceodore is at the centre of the story. Players can choose which character chapters to play on the way to the finale. Battles keep Final Fantasy IV’s Active Time Battle system and let party members combine their abilities. The phase of the moon also affects battles.

development.text: The mobile team approached producer Takashi Tokita while he was working on the DS remake of Final Fantasy IV. A phone sequel could follow quickly after that remake. The team chose 2D sprites to keep the hardware requirements low and retain the look of the original.
The separate episodes gave the returning characters room for their own stories. Tokita described working out where each episode fit and how much of the larger plot it could reveal.

release.text: The Java edition reached SoftBank 3G phones through Yahoo! Keitai on 4 November 2008. The prologue was free, with Square Enix listing paid content at ¥315–¥525. DoCoMo’s i-mode edition and au’s BREW edition had launched earlier that year.
Square Enix reported two million paid downloads by the time the SoftBank version launched. That was a milestone for the existing mobile releases, before SoftBank players could have contributed.

quotes.text: We spent a lot of time figuring out where to fit each episode or how much to reveal per tale.
quotes.speaker: Takashi Tokita

galaxy-on-fire.deck: Take freelance jobs in the outer reaches of Terran space, then spend the pay on a ship worth keeping.

overview.text: You start with a scout ship and a choice of ways to make money. Escort a freighter, join a Terran attack or scoop up cargo for sale back at the carrier. You can sink the money into better weapons and equipment, or trade up to an entirely different ship.

development.text: Hans-Christian Kühl took his pitch for an open-world space game to the owners of Fishlabs. The studio started on Sony Ericsson handsets with HI Corporation’s Mascot Capsule engine, then wrote its own middleware to improve how the 3D game looked and played.

release.text: Gamescom coverage and MobyGames date the first Java edition to 2005. In September 2006, Game Developer described Galaxy on Fire as a release from earlier that year, and Pocket Gamer reviewed the 3D Java game. I-play picked it up the next month, following Fishlabs’ earlier agreement with Arvato Mobile.
Pocket Gamer also mentions a 2D edition for handsets that could not run the 3D game. Its review and praise for the graphics apply to the 3D version.

quotes.text: Everybody told us, don’t make such a long, complicated game, but it worked
quotes.speaker: Michael Schade
quotes.attribution: Fishlabs co-founder, speaking to Computer Graphics World in 2006

galaxy-on-fire-2.deck: A bad hyperdrive drops Keith Maxwell into unfamiliar space with a mining ship and a long way home.

overview.text: A salvager pulls Maxwell from the wreck after a hyperdrive failure. His first ride back is a mining ship, and he can work his way into better hardware by taking station jobs. Escorting a convoy pays, and so does clearing debris or smuggling for a dealer who happens to have tentacles.

development.text: Fishlabs described fitting the Java game into about a megabyte. It assembled ships and stations from reusable parts and organized play around missions. For the later smartphone remake the studio could build distinct ship models and let players leave a station without signing up for a job.

release.text: Fishlabs was offering the Java game directly by March 4, 2009. You could start for free, unlock a longer trial by registering and pay after reaching a later point in the game.

gish.deck: Two keys let this ball of tar stick to ceilings or seep through cracks.

overview.text: Press * for grip and # to turn runny. You can cling to a ceiling, squeeze past a barrier, or flatten out before jumping to get a little extra height. Coins, fake walls and hidden tunnels give you reasons to return to a level after finding the exit.

development.text: Hardwire’s Ondřej Mocný developed the Java version and Erphenic’s Stefan Åhlin made its art. The game credits name Hardwire’s Bloft physics engine. Hardwire showed the Java physics in a trailer when the adaptation was announced in May 2008.

Hardwire told Pocket Gamer in July 2008 that the game would support the Zeemote JS1, a Bluetooth joystick. The reviewed Java edition also offered separate Bluetooth levels for co-op, deathmatch and races.

release.text: Pixalon Studios published the mobile game and GlobalFun secured distribution rights in 2008. Kath Brice’s Java review followed in April 2009.

quotes.text: Pressing the '#' key, for instance, changes Gish's consistency into a more liquid one, allowing him to pass through tight gaps.
quotes.speaker: Kath Brice

god-of-war-betrayal.deck: Kratos is framed for a murder in a phone game set between the first two God of War games.

overview.text: Kratos pursues the assassin who has framed him for the death of Argos. The chase takes him through a side-scrolling world with enough depth to keep the angled look of the console games. Marianne Krawczyk worked with the mobile team on the story, using the gap before God of War II to explain how Kratos’s relationship with the gods deteriorated.

development.text: Philip Cohen drafted the design in autumn 2005. Production began in August 2006, and the first high-end builds were done the following April. Low-end models needed two more months. Once the first six handsets were ready in June, the game went to the porting team.

Art director Nathan Leland’s team built a single set of background tiles and used palette swaps to make different environments fit within a few hundred kilobytes, and less on many phones. Philip Cohen said traps, animated scenery and enemies had to share that budget with Kratos’s fighting moves. Some levels were cut back to keep those moves.

Cohen borrowed the approach to finishing moves from the studio’s Casino Royale phone game. Betrayal originally put chests, levers and finishing moves on up. On a phone, a stray press could turn an attempt to open a chest into a jump into a trap. The team moved all three actions to down.

Production artist Jeremy Steiner worked on backgrounds, interface screens and sprite animation. Javaground’s David Frankel describes leading art and animation on his studio’s side of the collaboration. The Java credits also identify WayForward’s Chris Kerlegon as the artist and animator for Kratos.

release.text: Engadget saw the game at Sony Online Entertainment’s Gamer Day in May 2007. MobyGames records a June 20 release on both Java and BREW under Sony Pictures Mobile.

quotes.text: After that, the porting team took the game to over 200 handsets in a matter of weeks.
quotes.speaker: Philip Cohen
quotes.attribution: Producer and lead level designer, interviewed by Andrew Yoon for Engadget, August 29, 2007

credits.role: Writer who worked with the phone team
credits.scope: Phone game, as described by Cohen

studio_roles.role: Production, design, graphics, levels and QA

heroes-lore-wind-of-soltia.deck: Ronin leaves Basto with a basic sword, and his choice of elemental guardians determines what tricks he learns on the road.

overview.text: A trip to the Fire Temple draws Ronin into a search for Reah. The action RPG pairs short and wide weapon attacks with elemental guardians that gain experience alongside the hero. At a blacksmith or refiner you can combine materials and upgrade your equipment. Completing Ronin’s story opens another character’s route.

development.text: Woongchul Ko led the project and worked on the design. Ryu Hyoung-Seoc wrote the scenario and also designed the game. The credits list a map-tile team separately from character art and illustration.

release.text: Game Donga dates the original Korean release of 영웅서기-솔티아의 바람 to December 2005. That edition ran on WIPI. Hands-On Mobile announced the European version through its Best of Korea programme, and Pocket Gamer reviewed the Java game in November 2007.
RPGFan reviewed the English release in October 2008 and found that vague quest directions and sparse explanations put some of the more involved systems out of reach.

credits.name: Lee Ka-Young
credits.role: Original characters, main art and NPC/monsters

studio_roles.name: Mforma Korea
studio_roles.scope: South Korean WIPI and international Java editions

metal-gear-solid-mobile.deck: SoftBank's 2009 Java release brought the original 3D stealth game to the Sharp 932SH.

overview.text: Solid Snake and Otacon investigate a facility making Metal Gear after the Shadow Moses incident. Konami's Japanese release shows Snake using the walls and his surroundings to get past guards. The Sharp 932SH was the SoftBank handset named for the release.

development.text: SoftBank expanded S! Appli so Java games could access OpenGL ES 1.1. Keitai Watch reported that the new format raised the JAR limit from 1 MB to 3 MB and allowed as much as 16 MB of heap. A trial of Metal Gear Solid Mobile was preinstalled on the Sharp 932SH.

Nokia credited Ideaworks3D and its Airplay SDK for the N-Gage edition. Designer James Blackham describes blocking out levels and guard routes in Maya, writing codec dialogue and using Lua triggers and timers for gameplay. Those accounts document work on the N-Gage project. A separate Java engineering credit roll for SoftBank has yet to surface in this pass.

release.text: The first Japanese release was on KDDI’s EZweb on January 31, 2008. Verizon was selling the game in the US by March 20, Japan’s i-mode release followed on June 2, and Nokia listed the N-Gage edition in December. On February 6, 2009, Konami released the Java S! Appli edition through Yahoo! Keitai on SoftBank for ¥525.

notes.text: The archive records two files labelled as Japanese J2ME releases. The carrier coverage establishes the Sharp 932SH edition and the trial. It does not match either label to a specific official download or to the preinstalled trial.

credits.name: James Blackham
credits.role: Game design, chapter scripting and codec dialogue
credits.scope: N-Gage portfolio account, Java edition duties unverified

nowhere.deck: Lucas investigates a small town by day. In his dreams, a man who looks just like him is trying to make it out of the woods.

overview.text: Lucas keeps falling into the same dream, where he wakes as a man named John. While Lucas talks to people and looks for clues, John searches for weapons and tries to survive the woods. The story advances a little further each time the two lives cross.

development.text: The Java credits name Etienne Périn as the game’s creator and Florian Masereel for the original idea. Masereel also worked on programming and music. Périn came to DeValley after years at Gameloft, where he had worked on Java phones. He later told Gamekult about moving from graphics into design on the earlier puzzle game Ari Aro.

release.text: In December 2007 Pocket Gamer reported that In-Fusio was pitching a horror game about hiding in shadows, with a release expected in January. The game appears under the names Les Ames Maudites and Shadow Fear in later cataloguing. HCL’s July 2008 review describes both the joystick and number-key controls.

orcs-elves.deck: Fountainhead turned Doom RPG’s engine into a dungeon crawl, then rebuilt much of it to fit lower-end Java phones.

overview.text: An elf and a talking wand enter Brahm Hall, a dwarven stronghold overrun by orcs. Taking a step or casting a spell gives the enemies a turn. A map records explored corridors, and the quest log keeps track of things such as codes for locked doors.

development.text: Katherine Anna Kang’s team built the high-end BREW version first. In her 2006 postmortem, she described reducing a 3,555 KB footprint to 279 KB for a low-end Java target. The team removed floor and ceiling textures and made one enemy out of an inverted version of another. Low-end ports also lost a whole level.

Fountainhead spent five months on lower-end ports after six months on the high-end game. Kang singled out the Motorola V551. It kept an extra copy of the RGB buffer in memory, and dealing with that handset took two months. For the sequel, the team would start with the low-end target.

release.text: EA announced a May 9, 2006 start on Verizon Get It Now. That is the first handset rollout in the announcement. In December 2006, Pocket Gamer reported a February 2007 European rollout and published its Java review on February 19.

quotes.text: We wanted something that would play well with one hand, so it's not fighting the cellphone like so many games are.
quotes.speaker: John Carmack

credits.name: Katherine Anna Kang
credits.scope: Original game and Java porting account

orcs-elves-ii.deck: A novice thief gets a fantasy RPG built from the low end up after Fountainhead's first Java port forced painful cuts.

overview.text: The sequel follows a novice thief trying to save his village. The first dungeon teaches the controls, then a dwarven town gives you people to bargain with, equipment to buy and smaller quests to take on. Those first levels let you spend time developing your character before the heavier dungeon crawl.

A mouse named Bob can scout from his own first-person view. If you steal and end up in jail, Bob is one way out. A guard may be frightened of him, while a different cell might call for a lockpick or another prisoner’s help.

development.text: Katherine Anna Kang outlined a change in approach in 2006. The first game began on high-end BREW hardware and needed substantial work to fit lower-end phones. On the sequel, the team planned to build for the lower-end targets first and add visual detail for more capable handsets.

release.text: Electronic Arts announced on December 3, 2007 that the sequel was already available on most North American carriers and was expected in Europe in early 2008. That announcement covers mobile releases together. Pocket Gamer previewed the Java edition on March 27, 2008, and reviewed it on April 8.

credits.name: Rich Douglas
credits.role: Design, music and sound, credited as Richard Douglas

prince-of-persia-the-sands-of-time.deck: On the Sony Ericsson Z600, learning to wall-run meant learning when to keep the 2 key held down.

overview.text: The Prince climbs, fights and works his way through trapped rooms in Gameloft’s side-scrolling version. In the Sony Ericsson Z600 build, the wall-running ability is picked up in the second level. Jump with 2 and keep it held to carry the Prince along a nearby wall.

development.text: The Nokia 6101 credit roll distinguishes Ding Xue Song’s original design and production work from Tran Thai Nhan’s work on the handset port. Philippe Arsenault is listed for original sound design.

release.text: The J2ME listing dates the game to 2003. Game Over Online reviewed the Java edition in November 2004. The reviewer described the approximately 100 KB download as worth paying attention to if you were on a limited data plan.

notes.text: GameSpot’s July 2004 review mentions a code that unlocks a bonus in the PC game and attributes it specifically to BREW.

prince-of-persia-warrior-within.deck: Two blades, a stamina meter and a record of your last button presses give Gameloft’s second Sands of Time-era platformer a different rhythm.

overview.text: Wall runs drain the Prince’s stamina. He can fight while swinging from chains, and the game teaches a new sword combination after each level. A small display records recent button presses so you can see where a combo went wrong.

development.text: The initial production credits name Cristian Soare and Dan Teodorescu as producers and co-designers with Adrian Dorobat and Paul Friciu. A separate Nokia 6280 block adds another production team. The review describes the Series 60 Java edition, where a separate arena puts the sword combinations through fifteen rounds.

release.text: GameSpot reviewed Gameloft’s mobile game on 1 December 2004. Stephen Palley picked out the extra animation given to traps and the way sound effects cut through brief bursts of music on Series 60 phones.

quotes.text: The environments are sharply rendered in a range of fairy-tale bright colors
quotes.speaker: Stephen Palley

ratchet-clank-going-mobile.deck: A Microcorp trap turns Ratchet and Clank into digital images and sends them through a 2D platformer.

overview.text: Clank’s helicopter pack helps Ratchet stay in the air. Ratchet can also wall-jump, grind rails and grapple at set points. Between levels, bolts go toward weapons, including a gun that can turn enemies into boars.

development.text: Handheld Games brought the pair’s console moves into four directions and an attack key. On the build Jeff Gerstmann reviewed, the 5 key handled both shooting and close-range wrench attacks. Lead artist and animator Ben Hopper’s portfolio includes the duo’s movement, weapon icons, a Node Map animatic and original designs for enemies such as the Patrolbot and Disconnect Drone.

release.text: Release records list both Java and BREW in 2005. GameSpot’s 2006 coverage includes a review in March and a hands-on on the Nokia 6620 in May. Gerstmann liked the controls and found the short campaign only picked up in difficulty toward the end.

resident-evil-uprising.deck: Claire Redfield and Leon Kennedy return to Raccoon City in an isometric version of Resident Evil 2.

overview.text: In the Java game you can change between Claire and Leon in the menu. They cross Raccoon City on a grid, which affects how you fight. A zombie following the same grid can be lined up in your path before you shoot, and narrow corridors constrain where either character can go.

development.text: Capcom presented Uprising as a new take on Resident Evil 2 for phones. The isometric layout changes how you move and aim. Contemporary screenshots published by Mobile Gamer Brasil trace back to Capcom Mobile’s promotional slideshow and show the phone game before release.

release.text: Pocket Gamer covered Capcom’s announcement in May 2009 and reviewed the Java game in November. Later that month Capcom and Gameloft announced a distribution deal covering Europe, the Middle East and Africa, with Uprising among the games slated for that distribution window.

studio_roles.name: Capcom Mobile
studio_roles.role: Announced the game and licensed it for regional distribution

sid-meier-s-civilization-v-the-mobile-ga.deck: Gameloft brought Civilization’s hex grid, diplomacy and city building to a number keypad.

overview.text: The campaign’s fourteen chapters take you from early conflicts to managing an empire. Move a cursor over the hex grid and use the 5 key to select a unit or take an action. Units move a limited distance each turn, so getting them into position takes planning.

development.text: Gameloft made the phone adaptation. The Java edition credits Alexey Yegorenkov as producer, Alexey Garkavcev and Igor Boyko for design, and Stepan Gurzhiy as lead programmer.

release.text: Gameloft announced the adaptation as part of its second-half 2011 feature-phone lineup. When Keith Andrew reviewed the Java version that September, he found the goals varied and the controls difficult to navigate.

quotes.text: finding your way around a series of complex button presses and menu systems overloaded with texts is rarely a smooth process
quotes.speaker: Keith Andrew

silent-hill-mobile-2.deck: A hospital adventure told through hand-painted-looking rooms, a cursor and a shaking crosshair.

overview.text: You wake up in a derelict hospital and have to piece together why you are there. The rooms appear as fixed first-person views. Moving the cursor around them reveals objects and puzzles. When you draw a gun, the crosshair shakes and each shot kicks it away from the target.

development.text: The game credits name Konami’s European mobile group, Gamefederation Studio and INK Technology. Pocket Gamer’s reviewer praised the logical puzzles and the tension of those short fights. He was less patient with the loading when opening and closing the map, which he reported had carried over from the first mobile game.

In the credits, Gamefederation lists programmers and artists across separate roles. With the first-person views held still between steps, the location art carries much of what the player has to pick out. Spanner Spencer’s review points to a trade-off: the scenery helps the tension, while the brief black transitions can make it easy to lose your bearings.

release.text: Konami showed the Java sequel at Games Convention in August 2008. Silent Hill Memories dates the release to September. Pocket Gamer published a fuller review in November.

silent-hill-mobile-3.deck: Vincent returns in the last of the Java trilogy, with an added timing mechanic when the monsters appear.

overview.text: Vincent wakes in a mansion with ties to the earlier phone games. Most of the opening is spent investigating rooms from fixed first-person views. Later the game shifts toward combat and asks you to press 5 as two crosshairs align to hit a monster’s weak point.

development.text: The 2009 announcement described a return to still-image exploration interrupted by short first-person fights. Hardcore Gaming 101 and the Java directory attribute the third game to Playsoft. Gamefederation Studio made the first two, with a credit roll available for the second.
In his Java review, Will Wilson liked the drawn interiors and the tension of the long quiet opening. He found that searching highlighted objects too often came down to guesswork.

release.text: Konami’s announcement pointed to spring 2010. Silent Hill Memories records a March release, and Pocket Gamer reviewed the Java game on March 17.

studio_roles.name: Playsoft
studio_roles.role: Developer listed in retrospective and Java records
studio_roles.scope: Java edition; original credit roll pending

silent-hill-orphan.deck: Three survivors return to an abandoned orphanage in a first-person Silent Hill built for Java phones.

overview.text: Ben returns to the orphanage thirty years after the deaths of most of its children. Move a cursor over the scene to look for clues, pick up items and pass through doors. The game follows three survivors, returning to the orphanage through different characters’ stories.

development.text: On the Nokia N76 preview build, the directional keys moved a cursor instead of walking the character directly. The cursor signals when a door or object can be used. The Java credits identify Gamefederation’s creative director Pelle Stafshede, designer Pelle von Koch, lead programmer Evgeniy Seryshev and lead artist Anders Korodi. The end credits name INK Technology.

release.text: Konami showed the game at Leipzig in 2007. Silent Hill Memories lists a European release that September and a US release in October 2008. MobyGames records Konami as publisher and Glu Mobile as distributor for its UK entry.

sky-force.deck: Fly up the screen into formations of fighters and take on targets on the ground and at sea.

overview.text: Sky Force is Infinite Dreams’ vertical arcade shooter. The original handheld game sends a small fighter through waves of enemy craft and installations, in the tradition of Raiden.

development.text: Wicked Imp is credited with porting Infinite Dreams’ shooter to Java. Infinite Dreams marketed the port on its own site, where the purchase button called the Sharewire phone store.

release.text: 2006 is the listed year for the Java version. Earlier handheld releases date to 2004, and Infinite Dreams revisited the game for a 2014 remake.

sonic-jump.deck: Sega turned Sonic’s side-scrolling dash into a climb built around steering each bounce left or right.

overview.text: You steer Sonic from ledge to ledge, with springs carrying him higher and some platforms disappearing after one bounce. The screen only scrolls up. Miss a landing and fall below its edge and you’re back at a checkpoint.

development.text: Pocket Gamer played Sonic Jump at Sega’s E3 stand in 2006. The Sonic Jump Revival researchers distinguish two Java games: a GenPlay port of Sonic Team’s six-stage original and AirPlay’s new version with three acts per zone. The Glu edition reviewed in Britain follows the latter structure.

release.text: The original appeared for i-mode through Japan’s Sonic Cafe in February 2005. Glu’s Java edition followed in Britain in April 2007, after a showing at 3GSM. Pocket Gamer’s Stuart Dredge found the controls simple but thought there were too few checkpoints.

notes.text: The AirPlay game also used the title Sonic Jump 2 in some markets. Sega’s 2012 iPhone and iPad game reused the original title.

quotes.text: Sonic Jump is missing a key element that made the hedgehog an icon – the speed.
quotes.speaker: Stuart Dredge

studio_roles.name: GenPlay
studio_roles.scope: J2ME conversion of the original six-stage game

spider-man-doc-ock.deck: The Spider-Man 2 film tie-in puts three chases and fights on a phone keypad.

overview.text: Spider-Man runs on his own as you swing him between rooftops or fire webs. The second stage trades the city skyline for an oncoming subway train. The third asks you to web up Doc Ock’s arms. Once you have beaten the story stages, you can replay them in arcade mode.

development.text: Vicarious Visions’ Java credits name Eric DeSantis for design and art, Robert Gallerani for art, and four programmers. Shin’en Multimedia provided audio. Each of the three stage types has its own small set of actions. On the rooftops, one key swings a web and another shoots it.

release.text: Sony announced the game in March 2004 as part of a phone campaign for Spider-Man 2, initially exclusive to Sprint PCS Vision in the US for a limited time. The campaign included separate pinball, 3D and text-message games. Sony also advertised a code inside Doc Ock for Activision’s console Spider-Man 2.
Avery Score liked how quickly the controls could be learned. He found little reason to keep replaying the same three scenarios.

quotes.text: The game’s main strength is the use of a distinct, bare-bones control scheme for each of these levels.
quotes.speaker: Avery Score

the-dark-eye-swamp-of-doom.deck: The third Dark Eye phone adventure adapts a tabletop solo story, with encounters resolved through choices and character skills.

overview.text: Swamp of Doom was the third installment in The Dark Eye’s Java series. The series let players pick from preset characters and earn points to raise skills they could carry into later adventures.

development.text: The story comes from Sumpf, a solo adventure for Das Schwarze Auge. Frank Pfeifer is credited for the original text, Stefan Blanck for writing and adaptation, and Rainer Nagel for the English translation. Elkware and Chromatrix worked on the phone series.

release.text: Both MobyGames and the German DSA reference Wiki Aventurica date the Java adventure to 15 July 2003. Golem had reported in May that installments were planned for monthly release through the official site, mobile carriers and phone portals.

notes.text: Andresen spoke about the Java series at the launch of its first installment.

quotes.text: Unser Ziel war es, 'Das Schwarze Auge' so zu programmieren, dass die Mobilversion die Atmosphäre der bekannten Soloabenteuer einfängt
quotes.speaker: Jan Andresen
quotes.attribution: elkware managing director, quoted in Golem, 6 May 2003
quotes.translation: Our aim was to program The Dark Eye so that the mobile version captures the atmosphere of the familiar solo adventures.

the-elder-scrolls-iv-oblivion.deck: Vir2L and Superscape reworked the Oblivion story for a wider range of phones than their earlier Elder Scrolls games could reach.

overview.text: The phone version follows the same broad story as the PC and Xbox 360 game. The route through it is shorter, with small cutscenes linking the two versions. Choosing a class changes how you fight. A knight relies on melee weapons, while an archer attacks at range and a sorcerer can use spells.

development.text: Vir2L’s Douglas Frederick described a twelve-month production that had to fit the story, varied environments and a class system into a roughly 200 KB budget. Stormhold and Dawnstar had only reached 22 higher-end phone models. The new team built for both J2ME and BREW and aimed for about 75 models.

Greg Gorden returned as Elder Scrolls design director after working on the previous Elder Scrolls Travels titles. Superscape executive producer Brad Pitser oversaw development with Barking Lizards. Vir2L kept the main series name because the mobile game adapts an existing Elder Scrolls story, unlike its earlier Travels productions.

release.text: Contemporary carrier reports place the phone game on Cingular in November 2006 and Rogers by December 28. Those reports name the carriers. They do not identify every handset and launch date for the Java line.

quotes.text: We had to overcome the limited audiences of previous TEST games and release a title that could be ported to a wide variety of handsets.
quotes.speaker: Douglas Frederick, with Greg Gorden and Brad Pitser

the-sims-2-pets.deck: Adopt a puppy, teach it tricks and turn a happier Sim’s pay rises into better treats.

overview.text: The Java game opens with a choice of Labrador or Chihuahua. Feed it, take it to the park and teach it tricks. As you complete tasks, your Sim gets happier, earns more at work and can afford better food, toys and accessories.

development.text: Petting the dog, teaching it tricks and playing with it all use the same input: match a series of arrows on the directional pad before the timer runs out. The Java review describes an entire routine built around that input, with each task feeding back into the Sim’s ability to buy more for the dog.

release.text: EA planned a European phone release for late 2006. O2 advertised the Java game in December under an SMS download code. Pocket Gamer’s Mike Abolins thought the timed inputs and menu of chores made it difficult to feel much attachment to the dog.
EA Mobile also put out a separate N-Gage edition in June 2008. Nokia’s release had online rankings through N-Gage Arena.

studio_roles.name: EA Mobile
studio_roles.role: Publisher in O2’s Java release coverage

the-treasures-of-montezuma-2.deck: Match coloured tiles before the timer runs out and spend the gold you earn on upgrades.

overview.text: The mobile game sets tasks for each timed board. Making sequences of the same colour earns points and gold. The gold pays for bonuses that can help you finish later boards as you work toward rebuilding Tenochtitlan.

development.text: The Java credits put the phone adaptation with HeroCraft and Mobile-Games Ltd., and distinguish it from Alawar’s PC production. Oleg Tsyganov managed the project and programmed it with Victor Yarmola. Katya Kuznetsova and Olga Ulrich made the art.

release.text: MobyGames dates HeroCraft’s Java release to October 2010. In October 2011, Ukrainian carrier life:) announced a free HeroCraft edition on its portal for touchscreen phones. The carrier did not specify the runtime for its download.

the-witcher-crimson-trail.deck: Geralt uses two swords and magic signs in a side-scrolling Witcher game for phones.

overview.text: Breakpoint’s phone game sends Geralt through twelve stages across four settings, according to the Polish launch notice. The two swords, signs and combination attacks give him several ways through the same fight. The release material also lists three modes: Story, Adventure and Arena.

development.text: Breakpoint made the Java game under licence from CD Projekt. The phone credits name Paweł Krawczonek for game design, Dominik Wit for programming, Wojtek Ostrycharz and Tomasz Pacyna for art, and Piotr Pacyna for music.

release.text: Wiedźmin: Krwawy Szlak reached Play subscribers in Poland on October 1, 2007. Play handled Polish distribution for Breakpoint. Hands-On Mobile was named for Western Europe, South America and Asia, with MNI Premium channels announced for Central and Eastern Europe.

Samsung prepared a limited L760 engraved with the Witcher logo and loaded with the full phone game, themed ringtones, wallpaper and short clips. The companies used it as a contest prize around the launch.
Russian-language Witcher community coverage from October 15 lists the Nokia N73 among supported phones. Wakka’s input notes name that same model and a Russian copy.

studio_roles.name: Hands-On Mobile
studio_roles.role: Distributor for Western Europe, South America and Asia

tibiame.deck: Share an online world from a phone with nine inventory slots, one for each number key.

overview.text: TibiaME puts players on islands where they fight creatures, look for treasure and solve quests together. Ulrich Schlott described a backpack built to match a phone keypad. Pressing one of the numbers 1–9 jumped straight to its inventory slot.

development.text: CipSoft started experimenting on monochrome Java phones. Latency and differences between handsets put limits on the design. Schlott said players used Wi-Fi where they could to save money on data, or bought a monthly pass from a local operator.

release.text: CipSoft dates the first live service to May 12, 2003, initially on Symbian through T-Mobile. Pocket Gamer’s August 2007 interview places the Java client in August 2006.

quotes.text: The second problem was and still is the diversity of mobile phones and the many restrictions the manufacturers implement into them.
quotes.speaker: Ulrich Schlott
quotes.attribution: TibiaME product manager, speaking to Pocket Gamer in 2007

tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell.deck: Sam Fisher could wait in a doorway and grab a passing guard in Gameloft’s side-on version of Ubisoft’s stealth game.

overview.text: In the side-scrolling mobile game, Sam Fisher can cross overhead gaps, skirt lasers and hide in doorways while guards pass. The rooms are smaller than in the console game, but watching the light and choosing when to come out of cover still matters.

development.text: The Java credits name Stanislas Dewavrin for production and level design, Nicolas Bouillet and Florent Steiner for code, and Edouard Albert and Stéphane Zettwoog for 2D art.

release.text: MobyGames dates the Java edition to 2003. GameSpot’s April 2004 mobile review describes the edition running on a Motorola T720 and singles out the sudden wash of orange when the game moves from the underground missions to the oil rig.

tomb-raider-elixir-of-life.deck: Lara tracks her employer to a Scottish castle, where a private museum is guarded by robots.

overview.text: With the Codex and cinnabar recovered, Lara goes after the person who commissioned both jobs. The final episode takes her to a billionaire’s Scottish castle, where she has to get past security systems and robots to find out what he’s planning.

development.text: Nick Reed, Glenn Broadway, Mike Tucker and Chris Lipscombe are credited again on the finale. Ben Schroder and Stefan Barnett are listed for art and Paul Zimmer for audio.

release.text: MobyGames places the original Java edition in October 2004 and the later ExEn edition in June 2005. In-Fusio announced its ExEn licence in November 2004 and credited the port to BeTomorrow.

tomb-raider-quest-for-cinnabar.deck: A commission to recover an ancient vase takes Lara from Egypt to a monastery in Tibet.

overview.text: Fresh back from Egypt, Lara is sent to a Tibetan monastery to retrieve a vase of cinnabar. She suspects that the ingredient may be connected to stories about Shangri-La and a valley whose inhabitants live forever.

development.text: The surviving credits pair Mike Tucker and Chris Lipscombe on level design, with Nick Reed on code and Glenn Broadway on design. Eidos’s Paul Sheppard is credited as producer.

release.text: Eidos expected the episode by the end of 2003, according to an October announcement about the Vodafone release of The Osiris Codex. MobyGames places the Java release in 2004. A separate BeTomorrow edition followed on ExEn.

quotes.text: We wanted to work with a developer who we felt understood the franchise and could translate Lara's world onto mobile technology as sympathetically as possible.
quotes.speaker: Simon Protheroe
quotes.attribution: Eidos technical director, Java announcement preserved by Tomb Raider Chronicles

tomb-raider-the-osiris-codex.deck: Lara’s first IOMO adventure follows a stolen alchemical text into an Egyptian tomb.

overview.text: An anonymous client sends Lara after the Osiris Codex just as the theft of another Egyptian manuscript makes the papers. The caverns give her room to explore and solve puzzles. GameSpot’s Damon Brown took several minutes to get through one early area even when he already knew the way.

development.text: Glenn Broadway designed the original mobile game and Mike Tucker laid out its levels. The Java credit transcription lists Nick Reed as programmer and three artists: Ben Schroder, Cameron Kerr and Stefan Barnett.

release.text: Eidos says The Osiris Codex went on sale through Vodafone live! in the UK on 2 October 2003 and topped that service’s sales chart later that month. Independent figures are unavailable. In November 2004 In-Fusio announced a separate ExEn edition of IOMO’s trilogy, produced by BeTomorrow.

notes.text: The UK carrier date comes from Eidos. MobyGames and GameSpot list different dates within 2003, with no demonstrated link to the UK Vodafone release.

quotes.text: The graphics are detailed yet clean, and the sparse sound effects give the game a nice atmosphere.
quotes.speaker: Damon Brown

tower-bloxx.deck: Stack the floors with one button, then find room for the tower in a growing city.

overview.text: A crane swings each floor over the last one. Land the drop accurately and more residents move in. In the city, some towers can go almost anywhere, while the tallest need a mix of lower buildings around them. Good timing gets the tower built. The city grid decides where you can use it.

development.text: Sumea’s team started with an idea about a train. The idea changed during brainstorming, and a designer drew a hand dropping a block onto a pile. The team turned that sketch into a throwaway prototype called Drop the Box, then tried paper and Excel versions of the city rules before programming them.

The prototype held people’s attention for about ten minutes. A senior designer and programmer spent three weeks refining how towers sway and floors collide, testing revisions every half hour to three hours. The team drew the city background in code to save space and scale it to different phone screens.

release.text: Digital Chocolate published the 2005 Java edition. Tower Bloxx won Best Puzzle Game at that year’s Mobie Awards. Years later, former Digital Chocolate designer Petri Ikonen pointed to its combination of brief sessions and a city that carried your progress forward.

quotes.text: After about ten minutes playing it, people started asking what else is there to do.
quotes.speaker: Mikko Kodisoja and Jeferson Valadares

wolfenstein-rpg.deck: B.J. Blazkowicz makes his escape from Castle Wolfenstein one keypad turn at a time.

overview.text: The first-person corridors are familiar from Wolfenstein 3D. Moving, shooting and using an item now take turns. While trying to escape the castle, B.J. can talk to prisoners and use the products of Axis experiments himself. Pocket Gamer singled out the humour and the way turn-taking made the keypad controls work.

development.text: id Mobile used the design it had established with Doom RPG. The original mobile production was developed for Java and BREW. Firemint later worked on the iPhone edition, whose touch controls and release date belong to that port.

The Java credit transcription shows how much of the team carried over from Orcs & Elves II. Katherine Anna Kang produced and designed, John Carmack and Brett Estabrook programmed, and Matthew C. Ross worked across design, art and sound. The Java roster also names Henk Nieborg and Andy Chang for artwork and Bill Brown and Christian Antkow for music and sound.

release.text: EA Mobile showed the game at E3 in July 2008. Time Extension dates the Java and BREW releases to 2008. Pocket Gamer announced a January 15, 2009 date for its readership and reviewed the Java game on January 14. Its report on the separate iPhone release appeared in August 2009.

worms-2007.deck: Rockpool’s turn-based Worms lets up to four people take turns on one handset.

overview.text: The teams take turns picking their way across destructible terrain. You can pan across the map before taking action, grab weapon crates or play challenges built around a jetpack or grappling hook. The solo game has its own training and mission modes.

development.text: Rockpool Games built the Java edition. Lee Cawley worked on both design and graphics, with Pete Brisbourne also credited for design. Paul Flint handled programming and Jake Rigby made the music and sound. THQ Wireless advertised 3D backgrounds on higher-end handsets and a 2D version for others.

release.text: Pocket Gamer reviewed the pass-the-handset version in May 2007. In October, it reported that T-Mobile UK had introduced a network multiplayer version through Games LIVE, using Terraplay’s service.

quotes.text: Our one real quibble is over the speed of it – moving your worms can be a bit sluggish, like they're wading through treacle.

paragraphs.text: In April 2001, Motorola, Nextel and Sun announced Java applications for the Motorola i85s and i50sx. When Nokia introduced the 3410 in March 2002, it called the phone its first mass-market handset that let independent developers offer Java applications. The color 3510i followed the same year and put downloadable games alongside picture messages and polyphonic ringtones in its sales pitch.

Getting a game depended on where you lived and what your operator carried. In October 2002, T-Mobile in the Czech Republic extended its Java games service from the Siemens MT50 to three Nokia models. Customers could choose a game through the phone’s WAP browser, on the web, or by SMS.

The Mobile Information Device Profile, or MIDP, gave developers a common set of Java interfaces for phones. Its 2000 specification was followed by MIDP 2.0 in November 2002. A game could be delivered as a MIDlet suite in a JAR containing the program and its resources. A second file, the JAD descriptor, could tell the phone where the JAR lived and let it check the download’s requirements before installing it.

With MIDP 2.0, a download page could point straight to a JAR. A server could also read the phone model from the browser request and show a menu tailored to that device. That helps explain why an old file collection might contain a JAR alone for one edition and a paired JAR and JAD for another.

platform.title: What changed from phone to phone

paragraphs.text: In Game Developer in 2005, Glu showed its Aqua Teen Hunger Force game running at 176×220 and 128×144. The two displays used the same binary. The code added space between the speed and angle meters on the wider screen, and the team built the backgrounds from shared art. On low-memory phones, the same article describes cutting features or drawing animations with fewer frames.

3D gave studios another device capability to work around. The Java Community Process published JSR 184 in December 2003. It specified an optional Java 3D package called M3G. A phone’s MIDP version could tell a developer which basic interfaces were present. Support for M3G still had to be checked separately.
